newsitem.title: UK: STEEL TO REIGN SUPREME FOR CAR BODIES -ACADEMIC.
newsitem.headline: STEEL TO REIGN SUPREME FOR CAR BODIES -ACADEMIC.

text.p: Steel is set to reign supreme in mass car body production for many years to come, but aluminium is an option for car bodies in small-scale production runs, said Professor D. G. Rhys of Cardiff Business School.

Rhys speaking at an LME seminar on Monday said an important part of domestic production in key economies -- 15 percent in Germany and 14 percent in Japan -- is generated directly or indirectly by the motor industry.
"Unless there is such a change in environmental legislation that it will effectively outlaw steel, no country in the world seems to want to put in place something that would destroy this," Rhys said.
Aluminium became an option in car bodies for production runs of 100,000 units a year or less, he said.
"The steel industry reigns supreme," Rhys said. "At the moment no vehicle maker in the world sees itself moving away in large numbers from steel bodies."
Rhys said the Japanese would insist on stable supply and price of aluminium before increasing its use in car bodies.
He did not foresee the wide use of aluminium in Japanese car bodies until at least the turn of the century.
The European car industry was entering a phase of unbridled competiton.
"Prices will remain pretty constant and they could start falling. The consumer will be calling the shots," he said.
In the United States, the market was moving from one dominated by three car makers to one with six to seven key producers while Japan effectively remained a "duopoly".
The prospects for aluminium in cars appeared best in North America where cars were generally larger than in Europe or Japan, therefore there was a greater need for light weighting.
"More and more aluminium is used to meet weight targets. That gives the U.S. an edge in using aluminium," he said.
The United States, Japan and Europe will continue to dominate car output for the next 15 to 20 years by which time India, China and Indonesia will become the new growth areas.
South Korea will be the only significant "stand alone player" until then.
The amounts of plastic was likely to peak at 16 percent of total weight, close to where it was now.
Rhys said that copper consumption in cars could, according to some car makers, increase by 100 percent with already 42 lbs of the red metal consumed in each car made by General Motors.
Lead consumption could increase if the electric vehicle took off and the use of magnesium was also promising.
But lead along with cadmium were so-called "black listed" metals because of environmental concerns.

Finally, Rhys said half of the products made available to the car industry by the steel makers were not available five years ago and that 20 percent of the basic car bodies were now made from higher value-added, special steels.
